questions.question: In the NgModule system, how many modules could a single component be declared in?
options: Zero — components never needed to be declared
Two: one for templates, one for logic
questions.explanation: A component had to be declared in exactly one NgModule before it could be used, then optionally exported for other modules to import.

questions.question: What is a key readability advantage of standalone components over NgModule-declared ones?
options: A standalone component lists its own dependencies directly in its `imports` array, instead of requiring you to go check its enclosing module
Standalone components don't support dependency injection
There is no difference in readability
questions.explanation: With NgModules, a component's available directives/pipes were determined by its module's imports elsewhere; standalone components make that visible on the component itself.

questions.question: What does `bootstrapApplication` take as its first argument, compared to the older `bootstrapModule`?
options: A root component, instead of a root NgModule
A configuration object only, no component or module
The exact same NgModule as before — nothing changed
questions.explanation: `bootstrapApplication(AppComponent, { providers: [...] })` bootstraps directly from a root component, replacing `bootstrapModule(AppModule)`.

questions.question: Why would a developer still need to understand NgModules today?
options: NgModules are required for all new Angular projects
Many existing production apps are NgModule-based, and some third-party libraries still ship an NgModule-based API
Standalone components were removed in the latest Angular version
There is no reason — NgModules are entirely obsolete and unused
questions.explanation: Angular supports both styles side by side, which matters for working in or migrating existing NgModule-based codebases and libraries.
